newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Krupp, Thyssen to forge steel pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Krupp, Thyssen to forge steel pact.

text.p: One day after German industry giant Thyssen vowed to fend off a hostile takeover by rival Krupp, the two said on Wednesday they would talk about forming a joint steel group that would be one of the world's largest.

Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp and Thyssen said they would hold eight days of talks aimed at a steel cooperation agreement that, if successful, would void Krupp's 13.6 billion mark ($8 billion) bid for Thyssen.
If the talks fail to reach a pact in the agreed time, however, the two would return to their original positions, meaning Krupp could renew its generous offer to Thyssen shareholders.

In a meeting with Thyssen chairman Dieter Vogel and North Rhine-Westphalia state premier Johannes Rau, the ambitious Krupp chairman Gerhard Cromme appears to have won at least a week to convince them that cooperation makes sense.
Hostile takeover bids are rare in Germany's cosy corporate culture and Rau had earlier denounced the Krupp bid as reminiscent of the "Wild West".
The reaction of workers fearing for their jobs, who stopped production at the Thyssen steel works in Duisburg for a second day, was lukewarm.
Thyssen Stahl chairman Ekkehard Schulz, at first jeered by the workers, said he supported their protest against the Krupp takeover attempt.

Newspaper editorials criticised the job cuts that could result from a merger, but the two steel makers said in their joint statement they had common problems that could be better solved by a larger entity.

A larger company might find it easier to reduce the chronic overcapacity seen as one of the European steel industry's main impediments. High production costs in Germany are also an obstacle shared by the two.

A wedding of the two companies' steel operations would produce one of Europe's largest producers in tonnage output. A broader merger, including Krupp and Thyssen's extensive engineering and capital goods businesses, would be much larger in sales terms than British Steel or France's Usinor Sacilor.

"A future-oriented concept, which was repeatedly considered in the past and has already led to successful joint ventures in the steel business, could solve the difficulties that both companies have in the steel sector," the joint statement said.
"This could lead on a partnership basis to a steel enterprise that takes a leading position in international rankings," it said.

On Tuesday Krupp launched a hostile bid for Thyssen, offering to pay 435 marks a share, or a premium of some 25 percent on Monday's closing. Shares were suspended from official trade on Tuesday and Wednesday but traded actively on the unofficial grey market.

With trade unions warning that up to 20,000 of the two groups' combined workforce of 190,000 were at risk from the plan, editorials focussed on its effect on a country already suffering post-war record unemployment.
The mass circulation Bild asked Krupp's Cromme: "Herr Cromme -- do you want to set our country on fire? Think about people more than balance sheets."

Referring to the so-called "economic miracle" of Germany's post-war recovery, it added: "It took half a century to build up our country...This was the work of humans made of flesh and blood, not accountancy and balance sheets."
But the Handelsblatt business daily noted that Cromme had already met with similar worker resistance in past efforts to reduce manufacturing capacity and in its 1991 takeover of the Hoesch group.
"In both cases he won. Now the man of action Cromme wants to crack the toughest nut of all," it said.
